---
title: "Hospital Infections and Population Burden: What Germany Shows"
subtitle: "Why a country with few infections per hospital patient can still carry a high burden"
author: "Amisha Vatsa"
date: "2026-10-08"
bibliography: references.bib
execute:
  echo: false
---

## The problem

Infections caught during hospital care add to illness, death and cost, and many of them can be prevented. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) place a heavy load on health systems, and prevention budgets are limited. Planners therefore need to know which infections cause the most harm, and how that harm compares with other diseases.

Counting cases alone does not answer that question. A common infection that rarely kills may do less harm than a rarer one that often does. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) address this by combining time lost to early death with time lived with disability. One DALY is one year of healthy life lost.

This post looks at a 2019 study that estimated the burden of five HAI types in Germany using DALYs [@zacher2019]. Germany records fewer infections per hospital patient than the European average, so you might expect a lower burden. The study found that the picture is more complicated.

## Where the evidence comes from

The estimates come from a point prevalence survey run by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control in acute-care hospitals in 2011 and 2012 [@zacher2019]. Each survey records infected patients on a single day across participating hospitals.

The study used three samples. The main German sample covers 46 hospitals and 9,626 patients, chosen to represent German hospitals by size. A larger sample of 132 hospitals was not selected to represent the country, so the authors use it to test how sensitive the results are. The European comparison uses 273,753 patients from 1,149 hospitals across 29 EU/EEA countries and Croatia.

The researchers converted each snapshot into an annual estimate using a simulation that ran 1,000 times. Each result is reported as a median with a 95% uncertainty interval, which spans the 2.5th to 97.5th percentiles of the simulated results. The authors also released their method as an open-source R package, so others can check and reuse it. The five infection types are pneumonia, urinary tract infection, bloodstream infection, surgical site infection and *C. difficile* infection.

## What the analysis found

@tbl-overall summarises the national estimates. Germany's median burden is 308.2 DALYs per 100,000 people, compared with 290.0 for the EU/EEA average.

| Measure             | Germany             | EU/EEA average      |
|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| New infections      | 592.1 (521.7–665.8) | 467.9 (456.2–480.2) |
| Attributable deaths | 20.1 (13.4–28.2)    | 15.3 (10.2–21.2)    |
| DALYs               | 308.2 (221.2–416.3) | 290.0 (214.9–376.9) |

: Estimated annual burden of five healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) per 100,000 people, Germany and the EU/EEA average, 2011–2012. Values are medians with 95% uncertainty intervals in brackets. {#tbl-overall}

The DALY intervals overlap widely, so the study does not show a clear difference in total burden on this measure alone. The gap in new infections is clearer, because Germany's interval does not overlap the EU/EEA interval at all. Germany's hospitals have a lower infection rate among patients, yet the population-wide rate of new infections is higher. The difference comes from how many people are treated in hospital.

Cases and burden are not the same thing. Pneumonia and bloodstream infections make up 28% of cases but 51% of DALYs, because they are more often fatal. Urinary tract infections show the reverse pattern, with 45% of cases but only 27% of DALYs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-burden
#| fig-cap: "Estimated DALYs per 100,000 people by infection type, Germany and the EU/EEA average, 2011–2012. Bars show median estimates and error bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Germany shows the representative German sample. Values from Table 2 of Zacher et al. (2019)."
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
library(ggplot2)

burden <- data.frame(
  infection = rep(c("Pneumonia", "Urinary tract", "Bloodstream",
                    "Surgical site", "C. difficile"), times = 2),
  group     = rep(c("Germany", "EU/EEA average"), each = 5),
  dalys     = c(86.1, 82.6, 72.2, 35.7, 25.9,
                109.8, 57.1, 76.2, 35.1, 10.0),
  lower     = c(42.1, 34.5, 38.3, 28.9, 2.5,
                55.3, 24.3, 52.6, 33.3, 0.9),
  upper     = c(145.1, 159.2, 129.0, 43.7, 61.2,
                170.5, 102.9, 104.8, 36.8, 19.2)
)
burden$infection <- factor(burden$infection, levels = unique(burden$infection))

ggplot(burden, aes(x = infection, y = dalys, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
                width = 0.2, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("EU/EEA average" = "grey70",
                               "Germany" = "#2E5F8A")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "DALYs per 100,000 people", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

@fig-burden breaks the burden down by infection type. The useful comparisons are urinary tract infection and *C. difficile*, where Germany's median is higher (82.6 compared with 57.1, and 25.9 compared with 10.0), and pneumonia, where it is lower (86.1 compared with 109.8). Bloodstream and surgical site infections are close to the European figures. The error bars are wide for almost every type, especially for *C. difficile*, so the ranking between countries should be read with caution.

The authors do not attribute Germany's higher figure to poor hygiene. Hospital-level infection rates in Germany are lower than the European average, and the authors suggest that good hygiene may partly explain this. The higher population figure instead comes from admissions. Germany admits a large share of its population to hospital, so a lower risk per patient, applied across many more patients, produces a higher burden for the whole population. The authors suggest that Germany's large number of hospital beds is a probable contributing factor, while noting that this needs further study.

## Conclusion

This answers the question raised at the start: a low infection rate per hospital patient does not mean a low burden for the population. Germany's median burden was 308.2 DALYs per 100,000 people, compared with 290.0 for the EU/EEA, although the uncertainty intervals overlap widely. The main driver appears to be how many people are admitted to hospital, not how well hospitals control infection.

For someone planning prevention spending, this changes the question. A country can have good hospital hygiene and still carry a high infection burden if admission rates are high. Prevention could therefore focus on two areas: infection control inside hospitals, for example on urinary tract infections, which make up a large share of cases, and reducing avoidable hospital stays. The study supports both, but it does not show that one matters more than the other.

Three limits matter for decisions. First, the figures come from a single-day snapshot in each hospital, and the larger sample gave higher estimates, so treat the national figure as a rough guide and plan for a range rather than a single number. Second, the severity weights come from European patients. Because German patients may be less severely ill than the European average, the DALY figures for Germany are more likely to be underestimated than overestimated, so the true burden may be higher than reported. Third, each infection is counted separately, so a patient with two infections is counted twice, which slightly overstates the burden. The full analysis is in Zacher et al. [@zacher2019].
